sections.heading: The translation of the relics of the Holy Protomartyr and Archdeacon Stephen

pairs.en: On the same day, the second of the month, the translation of the relics of the holy protomartyr and archdeacon STEPHEN.
*You have so many holy and marvellous things already, Sion —* *give the body of Stephen to Constantine's city.* *On the second came the translation of Stephen's body.*

After many years had passed since the martyrdom of the holy protomartyr and archdeacon Stephen — three hundred and four years — and after many Christians had finished their course by martyrdom, peace at last followed the storm, and freedom and quiet settled over the world. All the prisons were emptied of the Christians who had been held in them, and all the tortures of the tyrants came to an end, because the great Constantine was reigning — the most Christian and first emperor of the Orthodox.

Then the precious treasure was also brought to light: the all-holy relics of the protomartyr and archdeacon Stephen. It happened this way. A man was living in the village where the protomartyr's relics lay hidden — old in years, a priest by rank, and a man of reverent life — named Lucian (or Lucillian). To this man Saint Stephen appeared two and three times, and showed him the place where his relics were hidden. The priest told the vision to the then patriarch of Jerusalem, John; and John, filled with great joy, went to the place that had been pointed out, with his clergy, and digging there he found the casket that held the holy relics.

At once there was a great earthquake, and a great fragrance that scented everyone present; and from the heavens above, angelic voices were heard saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men.” Those voices were heard as far as ten measures of ground away; and healings were worked among those who suffered from all kinds of illnesses, proclaiming the grace of the protomartyr.

So when the patriarch, with all the clergy and the laypeople who happened to be there, had venerated that holy body with joy and gladness, they lifted it with lamps and psalmody and incense, and so with all the honour that was due they brought it into Jerusalem and laid it in holy Sion. After that a certain senator, named Alexander, built a church in the name of Saint Stephen inside the city of Jerusalem; and after much pleading he persuaded the patriarch John to lay the holy relics in that church.

When five years had passed, Alexander the founder of the church fell ill; so he had a casket made of peach-wood, like the one that held Stephen's relics, and set it next to that one; and when he died, his body was laid in the new casket. Eight years later, while the great Constantine was reigning and the godly Metrophanes was patriarch of Constantinople, the wife of the late Alexander — her name was Juliana — was being pressed by many men to marry again, because of her wealth and her beauty; but she would not. So she decided on this plan: to take her husband's body and go to her father and to her homeland, Constantinople.

She went to the then patriarch of Jerusalem, Saint Cyril, and begged him to let her take the casket that held her husband's relics; but Saint Cyril would not let her take it. So she wrote to her father about the matter, and through her father's help the emperor sent a *sacra* — that is, an imperial order — giving her leave to take her husband's relics and go up to Constantinople. Since the patriarch could no longer resist, he gave the woman leave to go and take it. But by divine providence she was mistaken; and because the two caskets looked alike, instead of taking her husband's she took the other one — the one that held the relics of Saint Stephen. She set that casket on a seat, loaded the seat on a donkey, and began the journey to Constantinople.

All night long, as far as ten measures of ground, angelic hymns were heard in the air, and a fitting doxology: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men.” Those regions filled with the fragrance of a rich and most sweet myrrh; and the demons, weeping from far off, kept crying, “Woe to us!” — that Stephen was passing through their midst and wounding them unseen. When the woman reached the coastal city of Ascalon she found a ship, paid a fare of fifty florins, and set out from there for Constantinople.
As for the miracles that happened along the road, and the signs that were worked, it is impossible to write them down — we are keeping this short.

When the woman reached Constantinople and word reached the emperor's ears that the relics of the protomartyr Stephen were coming, and when he was also told about Alexander's wife — who stood before him and told the whole story accurately, from beginning to end, in her own living voice — then the most devout emperor Constantine, hearing these things, was filled with joy and gladness. So he ordered the patriarch and the whole clergy to go out and meet the holy relics with the greatest honour and reverence, and so to bring them into the imperial palace.

The miracles that happened then no one could describe exactly. The mules drew the cart on which the holy relics lay, until they reached a place called Constantianae — and there they stopped. When the drivers beat the animals to make them go on, one mule spoke with a human voice and said: “Why are you beating us? The holy relics must be laid here.” Hearing that voice, the patriarch and everyone present gave loud glory to God; and when the most faithful emperor learned of it he was struck with wonder, and at once he built a church on that spot in the name of the protomartyr, to the glory and praise of our Lord Jesus Christ. In that church the gathering and feast of Saint Stephen is kept every year. The finding of this Saint Stephen's relics is kept on the fifteenth of September; his own memory, on the twenty-seventh of December. (Note that a discourse on the translation of Saint Stephen's relics survives in the Great Lavra; it begins: “And how could anyone free us from blame and reproach?”)

sections.heading: The finding of the relics of Saints Maximus, Dadas and Quintilian

pairs.en: On the same day, the finding of the relics of the holy martyrs MAXIMUS, DADAS and QUINTILIAN.
*The earth, bringing forth three life-bearing dead,* *seems to say to heaven: “You hide them — keep them.”*

These saints lived in the reigns of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, in the year 296, in a city called Dorostolon, in the land of Second Moesia. Brought before the consul Tarquinius, and refusing to sacrifice to the idols, they were flogged; then they were taken to a place called Ozobia, and there they were beheaded on the thirteenth of April. Their relics lay hidden for many years. Later they were brought to light through a holy angel, on this second day of the month of August; and to this day they rest in the house of our most holy Lady the Theotokos, in the place called Biglentios, where their gathering and feast is kept. (See also about these saints on the thirteenth of April.)

sections.heading: The dedication of the church of Saint John the Theologian

pairs.en: The anniversary of the dedication of the holy church of the holy apostle and evangelist JOHN the Theologian, near the most holy Great Church.
We remember the holy martyr PHOCAS.
*Phocas the martyr, leaving the place of earth,* *now dwells in the place of delight.*
We remember the emperor JUSTINIAN, who came to a devout end, kept at the Holy Apostles.
*Your sceptre was no hindrance to you, O king —* *for you dwell in the kingdom above.*

The calendar of the Ecumenical Patriarchate commemorates on this day also Theodore of Dardanelles, Plegmund, Photini the Cypriot, and Basil the Fool — whom Nikodemos does not carry in his Synaxarion of 1868.
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.

Niketas the Rhetor, in his historical discourse on the finding of Saint Stephen's relics, records this: that the wise Gamaliel, the teacher of the Apostle Paul — whom the godly Luke mentions in the Acts, and who was also a kinsman of Saint Stephen (some say he taught Barnabas and Stephen as well) — knowing Stephen's virtuous life, begged the holy Apostles and they gave him Stephen's holy relics. Gamaliel laid them in the burial-place he had prepared for himself, in his own village, about twenty miles from Jerusalem; and the Apostles went with him and buried them there.

Then Nicodemus, Gamaliel's nephew — the same who went by night to Jesus and was taught the things of salvation by him — was cut to the heart at Stephen's burial, begged the chief Apostle Peter, and was baptised by him. When the Jews learned of this they anathematised Nicodemus, beat him with many bitter blows, and plundered his goods. Gamaliel, being Nicodemus's uncle, took him into his own house; but Nicodemus died of those wounds and became a martyr of Jesus, and Gamaliel buried his relics next to those of Saint Stephen.

After that Gamaliel himself was baptised. (The godly Chrysostom adds, in Homily 19 on the Acts, that Gamaliel believed before Paul; some say he was baptised by Peter and John.) The Apostle Barnabas was also a pupil of this same Gamaliel, as Clement the Stromateus, Eusebius and Epiphanius note — see the eleventh of June. Likewise Gamaliel's son Abibus was baptised: a young man of about twenty, handsome, virtuous and wise, and above all a virgin and pure. A little later both of them died piously and devoutly, Gamaliel and his son; and the relics of both were buried next to those of Saint Stephen and Saint Nicodemus.

When the time came for Stephen's relics to be brought to light, the godly Stephen appeared to the priest Lucian wearing a white sticharion covered with the letter sigma — which stood for the name Stephen — and that sigma was red and gold. The saint's hair was fair and golden, falling to his shoulders; he wore sandals bound with gold straps; and he held a golden staff in his hands, with which he touched the priest three times and called him by name. He told him where his relics were buried, and added that next to him lay also the relics of Nicodemus, of Gamaliel, and of Abibus his son.

So when they dug the place they found the four caskets in which the relics of Saint Stephen and the other three had been laid. On each casket the name of the one within was written in the Syrian tongue. But Saint Stephen's casket moved of itself, and a great light was around it, and a great fragrance came from it; and there was a fearful earthquake. The patriarch of Jerusalem, with all the clergy and the people, took the relics of Saint Stephen, brought them into Jerusalem, and laid them in the altar of holy Sion. Those who saw that holy body said that the wounds made by the blows of the stones shone like the stars of heaven.

Theophanes and Kedrenos record that Theodosius the Younger sent a great alms to the archbishop of Jerusalem to be shared among the poor, and a golden cross set with precious stones to be placed at the place of the Skull. The archbishop of Jerusalem also sent the right hand of this Saint Stephen the protomartyr to the emperor's sister Pulcheria. When the hand reached Chalcedon, Saint Stephen appeared to Pulcheria and said: “See — you have obtained what you desired; I have reached Chalcedon.” So she went out with the emperor to meet the relics; and later she built a church of the protomartyr, in which she laid that fragrant treasure, in the twentieth year of the reign of her brother Theodosius. (See page 311 of the Dodekabiblos.) Perhaps the right hand remained in Jerusalem, and it was not the whole body of the saint that was translated to Constantinople.

In the manuscript Synaxarist the entry for Justinian is written of Justinian the New — that is, the second, called Rhinotmetos, who came to the throne in the year 685. Perhaps the great Justinian is not named in the manuscript because he fell into the heresy of the Aphthartodocetae, and for that reason died a sudden death. The blessed Dositheos of Jerusalem, defending the great Justinian, says that he fell into that heresy out of ignorance (as some of the saints also have done), since his orthodoxy in everything else is known in many and various ways. The long footnote continues onto the third of the month.
